items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: So we hooked up with George Wein who then was running Storyville... So we went to George and asked if we could ask some people who were appearing at Storyville to come to Brandeis. He said, “You can do it, get anybody you want.

ctx.x: Well you must have been on your way to becoming pretty hip yourself, even maybe you didn’t even realize it.

I had no thoughts at that time of becoming in any way professionally involved in the music, but I was — it was like 52nd Street was in its final stages, but it was still alive and it was no small thing to have Sidney Bechet at Jimmy Ryan’s and across the street maybe Charlie Parker if you were lucky and he was in town. And, you know, Billie Holiday at the Onyx Club. So there was still a lot going on. And this was, you know, still a vibrant time. There was downtown on weekends, there was the Stuyvesant Casino in…

not much more than a glorified messenger but I got to meet a lot of people and actually was talked into running for office at the American Newspaper Guild, a pretty left wing thing. I was a Wallace — Henry Wallace was running for president. That was that famous election when Truman — Truman and Dewey. And it was a great experience because I was working at Time Inc. I was at a nerve center there on election night, which was a studio where they were broadcasting, and there was a guy named H.V. Kaltenborn, who was —…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We decided that we wanted to bring some jazz to Brandeis. So we went to George Wein... He said, 'Sure.' ... We made him an offer. ... So we brought Getz in.

ctx.x: We were going to pick up with your enrolling in Brandeis without your knowledge.

I came in the middle of the academic year. I had gotten out of the Army in January. So right after the winter break I arrived at Brandeis. It was very small then. The first class had just graduated. That was the class of 1952. They had just graduated the previous fall. It was still very small, about 700 undergraduate students, and a great faculty. I quickly made some friends. I was older. I’m 24 now, right? Yes, I’m 24. Of course that was a little more than the average age certainly of incoming freshmen, but…

There was no jazz instruction at Brandeis, needless to say. It had a very good music department, with an all-star faculty of Harold Shapiro and the very gifted, excellent composer, who died very young, named Irving Fine. The titular was Leonard Bernstein, who came in once a week. He was known as the airborne professor, because he flew in from New York to give a lecture which was attended by practically everybody, because he was a brilliant lecturer. We decided – this small core of jazz fans – that since there was…

items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And Dan Morgenstern was there that day.

ctx.x: (laughs) We'll get to that one day. Where do I want to go from here? I think I want to talk a little bit about your sense of programming because I think it has a lot to do with that balance that you achieved between art and commerce. Your creative programming was in evidence long before the festivals began because I'm thinking about a week where you had Sidney Bechet playing, I think, in the Mahogany and Art Tatum working upstairs in Storyville, and you put the two of them together on a … is it a Sunday afternoon…

Well, as time developed, in my book as it says, we went to the Buckminster and we went back to Copley Square and then I took the room upstairs in the Copley Square which was not the original Storyville. The original Storyville was downstairs, which I put … I still love the traditional music, and I created Mahogany Hall and I had Storyville upstairs and Storyville upstairs was playing the more contemporary artists, and downstairs was the more traditional artists. So I'd have Art Tatum upstairs and Sidney Bechet…
it was just … the musicians loved each other. It was great. And Dan Morgenstern was there that day.
